question: What kind of tumor grows into nearby tissues and travels to other parts of the body?
explanation: Spot on! Malignant tumors are cancerous because they don't stay in one place—they can invade local tissues and travel through the blood or lymph to other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the very first thing that happens during the initiation stage of cancer development?

options.A: The tumor develops its own blood supply to grow
options.B: Promoting agents cause the mutated cells to multiply rapidly
options.C: Malignant cells travel through the blood to distant organs
options.D: A permanent mutation occurs in the cellular DNA

explanation: You got it! Initiation is step one, where a harmful agent (carcinogen) causes a permanent, irreversible change right inside the cell's DNA. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which of these is a clear example of primary cancer prevention?

options.A: Starting chemotherapy for a diagnosed breast lump

explanation: Brilliant! Primary prevention stops a disease before it even starts. Giving vaccines against cancer-linked viruses like Hepatitis B is a classic way to protect the body early. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: A patient asks how to lower their colon cancer risk through food. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Eliminate all forms of dietary fat from the daily menu
options.B: Eat more processed red meat and smoked foods daily
options.C: Increase intake of fresh vegetables and whole grains
options.D: Take high-dose iron supplements with every meal

explanation: Well done! Eating plenty of fiber-rich veggies and whole grains keeps the bowel healthy and protects against colon issues. Balance is key! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the main goal of secondary cancer prevention?

options.A: Managing chronic pain in end-stage terminal patients
options.B: Detecting cancer early before symptoms appear
options.C: Providing rehabilitative care after surgical removal
options.D: Stopping initial exposure to environmental carcinogens

explanation: Spot on! Secondary prevention is all about catching the disease early through screening tests when it is easiest to treat. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why must a patient still do a biopsy after a routine screening test comes back positive?

options.A: A biopsy is necessary to cure the disease without surgery
options.B: Biopsies are required by law before any medication can be prescribed
options.C: Screening tests are always completely inaccurate for internal organs
options.D: Screening tests only suggest risk and cannot definitively diagnose cancer

explanation: Exactly! Screening tests only raise a red flag or show a risk. A biopsy (checking actual tissue cells) is the only way to say for sure that it's cancer. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which low-cost test is commonly used in Nigerian primary health clinics to check for early cervical cell changes?
explanation: Correct! VIA (Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid) is quick, affordable, and works wonderfully in everyday primary care clinics where high-tech scanners aren't available. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why do many cancer patients in Nigeria often come to the hospital at a very advanced stage?

options.A: Government policies strictly prohibit early diagnostic testing
options.B: Malignant tumors grow much slower in tropical climates
options.C: Financial barriers, limited access, and reliance on traditional remedies
options.D: Early screening tests are overly accurate and cause false alarms

explanation: Spot on. Distance to clinics, money constraints, and trying local herbs first often delay proper hospital visits until the disease has progressed. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h4)

question: In the CAUTION mnemonic for warning signs of cancer, what does the letter 'U' stand for?
explanation: You nailed it! The 'U' stands for unusual bleeding or discharge from anywhere in the body. It's an important red flag that needs checking. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: An older adult has had a nagging cough and hoarseness for three months that won't go away. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Instruct the patient to purchase over-the-counter cough syrup
options.B: Advise the patient to return only if they cough up blood
options.C: Report these findings to the clinician for further diagnostic evaluation
options.D: Reassure the patient that common colds often last for several months

explanation: Great clinical thinking! A cough that lasts that long without healing is a classic warning sign that needs a proper doctor's assessment right away. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h5)

question: What does the letter 'M' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?
explanation: Spot on! In the TNM system, M tells us if the cancer has traveled (metastasized) to distant organs far away from where it started. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is cancer staging so important after a patient receives a confirmed diagnosis?

options.A: It guides treatment decisions and helps determine the overall prognosis
options.B: It identifies the exact environmental toxin that caused the disease
options.C: It guarantees that the patient will achieve full remission
options.D: It completely replaces the need for any laboratory blood tests

explanation: You got it! Staging lets the team know how far the cancer has spread, which helps them choose the best treatment plan and understand what lies ahead. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of these is a key responsibility for a nurse working in public health cancer advocacy?

options.A: Organizing community awareness and teaching early detection methods
options.B: Diagnosing cancer stages without the need for pathology reports
options.C: Performing independent surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Manufacturing chemotherapy medications in hospital pharmacies

explanation: Brilliant! Nurses play a leading role in public health by educating communities, spreading awareness, and encouraging early screening. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)

question: A community nurse notices women in a village avoiding breast screening due to cultural fears. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Report the village residents to local government authorities for non-compliance
options.B: Insist that screening is mandatory under all circumstances
options.C: Ignore the cultural beliefs and hand out clinical pamphlets silently
options.D: Provide culturally sensitive health education and address community fears openly

explanation: Spot on! Building trust through gentle, respectful conversations and addressing fears openly is always the best nursing approach for community health. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T3#GNS321_U1_T3_h7)
